speaker: Maya Chen
transcript: Welcome everyone, and thanks for joining us today. My name is Maya, and I lead developer relations here. I'm joined by Dev, who has spent the last year building meeting agents in production.

speaker: Dev Patel
transcript: Thanks Maya. Today we are going to talk about agents that can actually sit in a meeting, listen, and do useful work afterwards. We'll cover why this is hard, how the pieces fit together, and what breaks when you ship it.

speaker: Maya Chen
transcript: Let's talk about why meeting agents matter in the first place. Most of the important decisions in a company are made out loud, in meetings, and then they disappear. The notes are partial, the action items are forgotten, and the context lives in someone's head.

speaker: Dev Patel
transcript: The biggest mistake developers make when building AI agents is assuming that giving an LLM access to tools automatically makes it an agent. Tool access is the easy part. The hard part is knowing what is happening in the conversation, who said it, and when it is appropriate to act. An agent that interrupts a meeting at the wrong moment gets removed from the call very quickly.

speaker: Dev Patel
transcript: Moving on to how the system actually works. First, a bot joins the call on Zoom, Google Meet or Microsoft Teams, just like a participant would. It records audio, and optionally video, and produces a transcript with speaker labels and timestamps. When the meeting ends, a webhook tells your backend that the recording and transcript are ready. Your agent never has to deal with the meeting platforms directly, which is where most of the pain used to be.

speaker: Maya Chen
transcript: And the timestamps matter more than people expect. If every summary, clip and action item points back to the exact moment in the recording, people can check the work instead of trusting it blindly.

speaker: Dev Patel
transcript: Let's look at building the agent itself. We use LangChain for the reasoning loop, and we connect it to the meeting tools through an MCP server. The agent can list recent meetings, fetch a transcript, and pull the recording, all as tools. Here's the rule we learned the hard way: keep the agent's job small and specific. An agent that writes follow-up emails is useful. An agent that tries to run your whole company from meeting transcripts is a demo.

speaker: Maya Chen
transcript: This next part is not public yet, so please don't share these slides. We are testing agents that speak in the meeting, and the early lesson is that latency changes everything.

speaker: Dev Patel
transcript: Now let's talk about what happens in production. A reliable agent is one that knows what to do when its tools fail. Transcripts arrive late, recordings are still processing, and meeting links expire. You should treat every external call as something that will eventually fail, and design the retry path before the happy path. The second lesson is observability. If you cannot replay exactly what the agent saw, you cannot debug what it did.

speaker: Maya Chen
transcript: And consent matters. Just because a meeting was recorded doesn't mean everyone agreed to have their words reused. Build the approval step into the product, not into a policy document nobody reads.

speaker: Maya Chen
transcript: Let's open it up for questions. The first question is about cost: how do you keep long meetings affordable?

speaker: Dev Patel
transcript: Good question. Cache the transcript once and let every downstream step reuse it, instead of sending the whole meeting again for each task. That single change cut our costs more than any model switch.

speaker: Maya Chen
transcript: Another question asks whether you need video at all.

speaker: Dev Patel
transcript: For most agents, no. Audio and a good transcript cover summaries and action items. You need video when you want to turn the meeting into clips people will actually watch.

speaker: Maya Chen
transcript: That's all we have time for today. Thank you all for joining, and we'll share the recording with everyone who registered.
